description: Southern red mite is a spider mite pest recorded on a wide range of plants including camellia, rhododendron, holly, and coffee. Individuals tend to inhabit the upper leaf. Pesticide resistance has been reported overseas, and typical two-spotted mite predators are ineffective against SRM.

appearance.color: Reddish brown to deep purplish-red, sometimes with a pale central patch and lighter legs
appearance.sexual_dimorphism: Females slightly larger, rounded posteriorly; males slender and paler
appearance.eggs: Reddish brown, spherical; normally on upper leaf surface, overwintering eggs mainly on lower leaf surface

life_cycle.population_peaks: Spring and autumn (moderate temperatures 15–30°C, dry conditions)
life_cycle.overwintering: Eggs on lower leaf surface and sometimes bark

dispersal: Wind-borne; may dangle from silk threads
damage_symptoms: Feeding on upper leaves causes mesophyll collapse, graying, and stippling
Leaves lose luster, appear bronzed or dull
Bronzing starts along midrib and veins, eventually covering entire leaf
Large populations cause severe leaf drop
Reduced plant vigor and growth, particularly on dry or water-stressed plants
detection_monitoring: Direct visual observation of damage, living mites, and cast-off skins
Plant beating on tray (white/black) for low populations
Observation of red eggs on host plants
chemical_control: Aldicarb, bifenthrin, chlorpyrifos, dicofol, omethoate, propargite, tau-fluvalinate, tebufenpyrad effective under certain conditions
Abamectin, chlorfenapyr, dimethoate, fenbutatin oxide, maldison not always effective
Late applications less effective; early application when populations low recommended
biological_control: Predatory mites (Neoseiulus fallacis) and ladybeetle (Stethorus punctillum) effective overseas
Predators such as Neoseiulus californicus and Phytoseiulus persimilis not recommended for SRM
Conservation of natural predators can help reduce populations
notes: SRM prefers upper leaf surface, moves lower as populations increase
Populations peak in moderate temperature and dry conditions
Australian commercial predators have not been tested against SRM
